extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques, quantifiers, and limits (introductory analysis/calculus)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal definitions for reading, negating, and using quantifiers; ε–N and ε–δ definitions of limits for sequences and functions, plus proof techniques and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate a quantified statement slide the negation past the quantifier: ∼(∃y ∈ R s.t. P(y)) ≡ ∀y ∈ R, ∼P(y); ∼(∀x, ∃y s.t. P(x,y)) ≡ ∃x s.t. ∀y, ∼P(x,y). Domains are unchanged by negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moving a negation left-to-right flip ∀ ↔ ∃ and negate the inner predicate. The text shows examples: ∼(∃y ∈ R s.t. 1/y = y + 1) ≡ ∀y ∈ R, 1/y ≠ y + 1, and for nested quantifiers carry the negation through each quantifier. Use the syntactic translation to produce a correct disproof (prove the negation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers do not commute
rubrics_metrics.description: Nested quantifiers generally do not commute: ∀x ∃y P(x,y) is not logically equivalent to ∃y ∀x P(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always respect the order of quantifiers; change of order can change truth value. The chapter uses two-player game analogies and explicit examples to demonstrate the difference (e.g., ∀z ∈ Z ∃w ∈ N z^2 < w is true, but ∃w ∈ N ∀z ∈ Z z^2 < w is false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-player game interpretation of quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret nested quantifiers as a game: Player 1 selects values for the outer quantifiers and Player 2 responds for inner quantifiers; existence/for-all correspond to who has a winning strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analogy to reason about truth/falsity and to construct proofs/counterexamples: Player 1 (∀) picks adversarially, Player 2 (∃) must respond knowing Player 1's choice. Examples: proving ∀z ∃w z^2 < w by letting Player 2 choose w = z^2 + 1; showing ∃w ∀z fails because Player 1 (who chooses w) cannot anticipate Player 2's later z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving falsity by proving the negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a quantified statement is false, prove its negation; a disproof is a proof of the negated statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the negation using the rules for negating quantifiers, then construct a proof (often by exhibiting choices that satisfy the negated quantifiers). The text repeatedly demonstrates this approach for nested-quantifier examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping explicit domains when context is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians often omit domain annotations on quantifiers when the domain is fixed by context (e.g., working in R or Z); sometimes the universal quantifier is implicit and omitted entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dropping domains or even the quantifier is standard but sloppy; ensure the reader can infer the domain from context. Examples: ∀x ∈ R, if x < −2 then x^2 > 4 can be written as 'if x < −2 then x^2 > 4' when R is understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of implication
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation of an implication is ∼(P ⇒ Q) ≡ (P ∧ ∼Q); it is not (P ⇒ ∼Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a common error—memorise the correct equivalence (Theorem 4.2.7 referenced). Also keep in mind: if the hypothesis is false the implication is true; if the conclusion is true the implication is true. Use P ∧ ¬Q when negating an implication in proofs/counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a sequence (as a function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence is an ordered list of real numbers (x_n)_{n∈N}; equivalently a function f : N → R with f(n) = x_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer defining a sequence by a formula for the nth term. Notational variants exist ((x_n), (x_n)_{n≥1}, etc.); avoid brace notation {x_n} to prevent confusion with sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal ε–N definition of sequence convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n) converges to L ∈ R iff ∀ε > 0, ∃N ∈ N s.t. ∀n ∈ N, (n > N) ⇒ |x_n − L| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-player interpretation (Player 1 picks ε>0, Player 2 finds N depending on ε). When writing proofs provide an explicit N (often using algebraic manipulation and ceiling) or argue existence via Archimedean/other properties. Examples: for x_n = 1/n choose N = ⌈1/ε⌉.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for proving convergence (choose N depending on ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove convergence, algebraically manipulate |x_n − L| < ε to find a condition n > N (usually N depends on ε), then set N (e.g., via ceiling) to ensure N ∈ N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You only need to show existence of some N that works; you do not have to explain how you discovered it. Ensure N is a natural number (adjust if ceiling gives 0 by picking a larger N). Examples: for x_n = (2n+4)/(n+1) reduce |x_n − 2| to 2/(n+1) < ε and pick N = ⌈2/ε⌉.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal negation for non-convergence to a specific L
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation of 'x_n → L' is: ∃ε > 0 s.t. ∀N ∈ N, ∃n ∈ N with n > N and |x_n − L| ≥ ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a sequence does not converge to L, exhibit a specific ε and, given any N, produce an n > N with |x_n−L| ≥ ε (e.g., for b_n = (−1)^n choose ε = 1 and n = 2N+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal statement for divergence (no finite limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence diverges (no finite limit) iff ∀L ∈ R, ∃ε > 0 s.t. ∀N ∈ N, ∃n ∈ N with n > N and |x_n − L| ≥ ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove divergence to no L, let L be arbitrary and produce an ε (often 1) and a rule to pick n > N so that |x_n − L| ≥ ε for every N (example: x_n = n, choose ε = 1 and n = max{N, ⌈|L|⌉} + 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal ε–δ definition of limit of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: For a real-valued function f, lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means ∀ε > 0, ∃δ > 0 s.t. (0 < |x − a| < δ) ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parallels the ε–N definition for sequences; interpret quantifiers similarly (for any tolerance ε, find a δ-neighbourhood of a guaranteeing f(x) within ε). Use algebraic manipulation to find a suitable δ depending on ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of absolute value as a metric/distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute value provides a metric on R: |x − y| measures distance; more generally other metrics exist (Euclidean, taxicab, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving limit statements use the appropriate distance notion (|·| for R). The text notes other metrics to orient the student toward generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give explicit constructive choices in existence proofs/counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof requires existence (∃) provide an explicit choice or a clear rule (e.g., choose w = z^2 + 1, choose n = 2N + 1, choose N = ⌈1/ε⌉).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit choices make proofs clear and avoid ambiguity. The chapter consistently exhibits explicit constructions for both convergence proofs and negation/counterexample proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure chosen quantities lie in the stated domains
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing values (N, n, w, z, etc.) ensure they belong to the required domain (e.g., N ∈ N, w ∈ N, z ∈ Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust choices if necessary (e.g., if ceiling(2/ε) equals 0 but N must be natural, pick a larger N such as max{1, ceiling(2/ε)}). Verify domain membership as part of the proof (the text checks w = z^2+1 ∈ N, z = w+1 ∈ Z, etc.).
